blocks.text: Underneath the user-facing commands, Git is a simple key-value store. You give it content, it returns a key (a hash of that content), and it stores the content under .git/objects. Everything, including every file version, directory listing and commit, is one of four object types.

rows: The raw contents of one file (no name, no permissions)
A directory listing: entries of mode, type, hash and name
One snapshot plus metadata: root tree, parent(s), author, committer, message
One tree and zero or more parent commits
A named, signed or annotated pointer: target, tagger, message

blocks.src: generate: object graph; three commit nodes in a chain C1 <- C2 <- C3 (arrows point from child to parent); each commit points to a tree; trees point to blobs and subtrees (src/); C2 and C3 trees share several unchanged blob nodes, drawn with arrows from both trees to the same blob; an annotated tag object v1.0 points to C3
blocks.alt: Commits pointing to trees, trees pointing to blobs, unchanged blobs shared between snapshots
blocks.caption: Snapshots share unchanged content: a new commit only creates objects for what changed.

blocks.text: git cat-file is the plumbing command for reading objects: -t prints the type, -p pretty-prints the content.

$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 8f94139338f9404f26296befa88755fc2598c289
parent 71a3e55c0f2b4a7d9e1c2d3b4a5f6e7d8c9b0a1f
author Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1727180000 +0000
committer Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1727180000 +0000

Add stock endpoint

$ git cat-file -p 8f94139
100644 blob a906cb2a4a904a152e80877d4088654daad0c859    README.md
040000 tree 1c2e3d4f5a6b7c8d9e0f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d    src
100755 blob 5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d7e8f9a0b1c2d3e4f    run.sh

$ git cat-file -t a906cb2

$ git cat-file -p a906cb2

rows: Symbolic link (blob contains the link target)
Gitlink: a submodule pointing to a commit in another repository

blocks.text: File names and permissions live in trees, not in blobs. Two files with identical content in different directories are stored as one blob. Renaming a file creates a new tree but reuses the same blob, which is why Git has to detect renames after the fact instead of recording them.

Every commit stores two identities. The author wrote the change; the committer last applied it. They differ after a rebase, cherry-pick, amend or when a maintainer applies someone else's patch. GitHub shows both when they differ, and the committer date, not the author date, changes when you rebase.
Building a Commit by Hand with Plumbing
The porcelain commands you use daily are built on plumbing commands. Building a commit manually shows there is no magic involved.

$ echo 'hello' | git hash-object -w --stdin
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a

$ git update-index --add --cacheinfo 100644 ce01362 hello.txt
$ git write-tree
aaa96ced2d9a1c8e72c56b253a0e2fe78393feb7

$ echo 'First commit, by hand' | git commit-tree aaa96ce
d6c8f1e...      # a real commit object, not yet on any branch

$ git update-ref refs/heads/main d6c8f1e

New objects are written as individual zlib-compressed files (loose objects) under .git/objects/ab/cdef..., where the first two hex characters form the directory name. Periodically, git gc (also triggered automatically and during push/fetch) packs them into packfiles, which delta-compress similar objects against each other. This is how Git keeps full snapshots of every version while using little disk space.

$ git count-objects -vH
count: 12
size: 48.00 KiB
in-pack: 3481
packs: 1
size-pack: 2.31 MiB

$ git gc

A lightweight tag is only a ref pointing directly at a commit; no object is created. An annotated tag (git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0") creates a tag object with its own tagger, date, message and optional GPG/SSH signature. Use annotated tags for releases; tools such as git describe ignore lightweight tags by default.
